name: Bernard Widrow
milestone_by_age_26: Widrow completed his PhD at MIT in 1956 at age 26 and joined the MIT faculty, but his defining work — the LMS algorithm and ADALINE neural network — came in 1959 at age 30 at Stanford; no material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Widrow grew up in Norwich, Connecticut, fascinated by electronics from a young age. He entered MIT in 1947, earned his BS in 1951, MS in 1953, and PhD in 1956, all in electrical engineering. His PhD work was on the statistical theory of quantization noise, not on neural networks.
family_context_summary: Born in Norwich, Connecticut; grew up in an academically focused family that valued curiosity and hard work. Interested in electronics from a young age.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as having direct family domain expertise in computing or engineering.
evidence_summary: Widrow's path through MIT (BS 1951, MS 1953, PhD 1956) was a strong academic trajectory, but his landmark contributions to neural networks — the LMS algorithm and ADALINE — were developed in 1959 at Stanford with his student Ted Hoff, when Widrow was 30. No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found beyond completing his doctorate and joining the MIT faculty.

name: Edgar F. Codd
milestone_by_age_26: Codd joined IBM as a mathematical programmer in 1949 at age 26, but his defining achievement — the relational database model — was published in 1970 at age 47; no material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born on the Isle of Portland, Dorset, England, Codd was the youngest of seven children. He attended Poole Grammar School on a scholarship and studied mathematics and chemistry at Oxford before serving as a pilot in the RAF during WWII. After the war he completed his degree at Oxford in 1948 and moved to New York to join IBM in 1949.
family_context_summary: Born to a leather manufacturer father and schoolteacher mother; youngest of seven children. Awarded a full scholarship to Oxford University.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a leather manufacturer; mother was a schoolteacher. No documented family domain expertise in computing or mathematics.
evidence_summary: Codd's early career involved working on early IBM computers (SSEC, IBM 701, 702) as a programmer, which was competent but not landmark work. His revolutionary relational model paper was published in 1970 when he was 47. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Michael I. Jordan
milestone_by_age_26: By age 26 (1982), Jordan had a BS in psychology (1978) and MS in mathematics (1980) and was a graduate student at UCSD; his PhD was completed in 1985 at age 29 and his influential ML work came in the 1990s; no material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in Aberdeen, Maryland, Jordan earned a BS magna cum laude in psychology from Louisiana State University in 1978, an MS in mathematics from Arizona State University in 1980, and a PhD in cognitive science from UC San Diego in 1985 under David Rumelhart. He joined MIT as an assistant professor in 1988.
evidence_summary: Jordan's academic path through LSU, ASU, and UCSD was solid but unremarkable by age 26. His foundational contributions to machine learning (latent Dirichlet allocation, variational methods, etc.) came in the 1990s and 2000s. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Judea Pearl
milestone_by_age_26: By age 26 (1962), Pearl had a BS in electrical engineering from the Technion (1960) and was working at RCA Laboratories; his PhD came in 1965 and his Bayesian networks work in the 1980s; no material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in Tel Aviv, Mandatory Palestine, Pearl served in the Israeli army and joined a kibbutz before studying electrical engineering at the Technion, graduating in 1960. He moved to the US with $56, working at RCA while pursuing graduate studies at Rutgers (MS in physics) and the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (PhD in electrical engineering, 1965).
family_context_summary: Born into a Jewish family from Poland in Bnei Brak near Tel Aviv. Credits his interest in science to growing up in newly independent Israel, taught by scientists who fled Nazi Germany.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as having direct family domain expertise in science or engineering.
evidence_summary: Pearl's early career involved practical engineering work at RCA on superconductive memory devices. His landmark contributions to AI — Bayesian networks and causal reasoning — came in the 1980s and 1990s, well after age 26. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Thomas Bayes
milestone_by_age_26: By age 26 (c. 1727), Bayes was serving as a Presbyterian minister; his famous work on probability was done much later and published posthumously in 1763; no material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born c. 1701 in London, the son of Nonconformist minister Joshua Bayes, Thomas was educated privately and matriculated at the University of Edinburgh in 1719 to study logic and theology. He became a minister at Mount Sion Chapel in Tunbridge Wells around 1734. His mathematical work, including the theorem that bears his name, was done in his later years and published posthumously by Richard Price in 1763.
family_context_summary: Son of Joshua Bayes, one of the first six Nonconformist ministers ordained in England. Came from a prominent nonconformist family from Sheffield. Educated privately, as was typical for sons of Nonconformist ministers.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a Presbyterian minister; no documented family expertise in mathematics, though Bayes may have been tutored by de Moivre who gave private tuition in London at the time.
evidence_summary: Bayes was a minister for most of his life; his mathematical work came later. He was elected FRS in 1742 (age ~41) and his famous theorem was published posthumously in 1763. No evidence of a material mathematical milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Pierre-Simon Laplace
milestone_by_age_26: Presented his first mathematical paper to the Académie des Sciences in Paris on 28 March 1770 at age 20, and within two years had presented 13 papers to the Academy, establishing himself as a leading young mathematician.
early_history_summary: Laplace attended a Benedictine priory school in Normandy and then Caen University, where he discovered his mathematical talent under teachers Gadbled and Le Canu. At 19, he went to Paris with a letter of introduction to d'Alembert, who was so impressed he secured Laplace a position as professor of mathematics at the École Militaire. From there, Laplace began producing a steady stream of remarkable mathematical papers from age 20 onward.
family_context_summary: Born in Beaumont-en-Auge, Normandy; his father owned and farmed the small estate of Mérisier, and his great-uncle had held the title of Chirurgien Royal. His father expected him to enter the Church.
parent_family_domain_summary: No documented family domain expertise in mathematics or science; father was a farmer/estate owner, great-uncle was a royal surgeon.
primary_early_advantage_tags: d'Alembert patronage, Paris mathematical ecosystem, exceptional talent, Enlightenment era
evidence_summary: Laplace's trajectory was catalyzed by d'Alembert's mentorship, which provided both academic direction and a professional position at the École Militaire. His exceptional mathematical talent was recognized immediately upon arriving in Paris at 19. Being in Paris — the center of European mathematics — gave him direct access to the Académie des Sciences and the leading mathematicians of the era. His middle-class Norman background provided enough support for education but no inherited scientific network; the network was built through d'Alembert's patronage.
starting_point: Born to a middle-class family in Beaumont-en-Auge, Normandy; father owned and farmed the small estate of Mérisier, and his great-uncle had held the title of Chirurgien Royal. Father expected him to enter the Church.
current_position: Died in Paris on 5 March 1827 at age 77; final role: Marquis de Laplace, chancellor of the Senate under the First French Empire, and one of the most influential scientists in history.

trajectory.event: Arrived in Paris and impressed d'Alembert, who secured him a position as professor of mathematics at the École Militaire.
Presented his first mathematical paper to the Académie des Sciences on 28 March 1770, beginning a steady stream of remarkable papers.
Elected as adjoint member of the Paris Academy of Sciences after two earlier failed attempts.
Named examiner at the military academy, where he examined a young Napoleon Bonaparte.
Published Exposition du système du monde, presenting his nebular hypothesis of the origin of the Solar System.
Began publication of Mécanique céleste, his five-volume masterpiece translating classical mechanics into calculus-based analysis.
Published Théorie analytique des probabilités, his foundational work on probability theory.
Died in Paris on 5 March 1827, recognized as one of the greatest scientists of all time.

name: Andrey Kolmogorov
milestone_by_age_26: In 1922 at age 19, constructed a summable function whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere, a result that made him an international celebrity; published 8 papers in 1925 while still an undergraduate, including his first paper on probability theory.
early_history_summary: Orphaned at birth and raised by his maternal aunt Vera in his grandfather's noble household near Yaroslavl, Kolmogorov entered Moscow State University in 1920. He was influenced by Luzin's research group 'Luzitania' and by Stepanov's lectures on trigonometric series. While still an undergraduate, he produced results of international importance, most famously his 1922 construction of a summable function with an almost-everywhere divergent Fourier series.
family_context_summary: Orphaned at birth — mother died in childbirth, father was absent. Raised by maternal aunt Vera Yakovlevna in the household of his maternal grandfather Yakov Stepanovich Kolmogorov, a member of the Uglich nobility. The family home was a center of clandestine printing during his childhood.
parent_family_domain_summary: No documented parental domain expertise in mathematics; mother's family was from the nobility but not specifically mathematical. Aunt Vera organized a home school for his early education.
primary_early_advantage_tags: exceptional mathematical ability, Luzin research group, Moscow State University, orphaned upbringing, peer network of exceptional mathematicians
evidence_summary: Kolmogorov's extraordinary mathematical talent was evident from his teenage years — he wrote a treatise on Newton's laws before university and produced internationally significant results at 19 while still an undergraduate. The Luzitania research group at Moscow State University, led by Luzin and including Aleksandrov, Suslin, and Urysohn, provided an exceptional peer environment. His orphaned upbringing and modest circumstances created urgency but did not prevent his rapid rise. The combination of prodigy-level talent and an elite mathematical ecosystem at Moscow State University was the dominant early advantage.
starting_point: Born in Tambov, Russia, orphaned at birth (mother died in childbirth, father absent); raised by maternal aunt Vera in his grandfather Yakov Stepanovich Kolmogorov's noble household near Yaroslavl.
current_position: Died in Moscow on 20 October 1987 at age 84; final role: Professor at Moscow State University, Head of the Department of Probability and Statistics at the Steklov Institute, and member of the USSR Academy of Sciences, regarded as the greatest probability theorist of the 20th century.

trajectory.event: Constructed a summable function whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere, becoming an international celebrity in mathematics.
Published 8 papers while still an undergraduate, including his first paper on probability theory co-authored with Khinchin.
Completed his doctorate at Moscow State University under Luzin's supervision.
Published Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung, establishing the axiomatic foundations of modern probability theory.
Published two fundamental papers on turbulence theory and received one of the first State Prizes of the USSR.
Awarded the Lenin Prize for his contributions to mathematics.
Awarded the Wolf Prize in Mathematics for his fundamental contributions to probability theory and analysis.
Died in Moscow on 20 October after a prolonged illness, having shaped modern probability theory and mathematics.

name: William Feller
milestone_by_age_26: Feller completed his PhD at Göttingen at age 20 under Richard Courant and held a docent position at Kiel from 1928, but his defining contributions to probability theory came in the 1940s-50s; no material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in Zagreb, Austria-Hungary, to a prosperous chemist father, Feller studied at the University of Zagreb (1923-1925) before moving to the University of Göttingen, where he completed his doctorate under Richard Courant in 1926 at age 20. He then held a docent position at the University of Kiel from 1928 until fleeing the Nazis in 1933.
family_context_summary: Born to a prosperous family in Zagreb; father Eugen Viktor Feller was a chemist and owner of a chemical factory who became wealthy from 'Elsa fluid.' Mother was Ida Oemichen-Perc, a Croatian-Austrian Catholic. William was the ninth of twelve children.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a prosperous chemist and factory owner, providing a comfortable upper-middle-class upbringing, but no documented direct family expertise in mathematics.
evidence_summary: Feller's PhD at 20 from Göttingen under Courant was impressive, but his thesis on algebraically rectifiable transcendental curves was not a landmark result. His major contributions to probability theory — including his influential two-volume textbook — came in the 1940s-60s. No material milestone by age 26 was found beyond completing his doctorate unusually early.

name: Joseph Doob
milestone_by_age_26: Doob earned his PhD from Harvard at age 22 in 1932 and held a postdoctoral fellowship at Columbia, but his defining work on stochastic processes came in the 1940s-50s; no material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in Cincinnati, Ohio, Doob entered Harvard at age 16, earned his AB in 1930, AM in 1931, and PhD in 1932 in mathematics. His thesis was on boundary values of analytic functions under J.L. Walsh. He held a National Research Council Fellowship at Columbia (1932-1934) before joining the University of Illinois in 1935, where he spent the rest of his career.
family_context_summary: Born in Cincinnati, Ohio, to Mollie Doerfler and Leo Doob. Interested in radio and science from grammar school, building his own crystal radio set and obtaining a transmit license.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as having direct family domain expertise in mathematics or science.
evidence_summary: Doob's early academic trajectory was strong — entering Harvard at 16 and completing his PhD at 22 — but his thesis on boundary values of analytic functions was not a landmark result. His foundational work on stochastic processes and martingale theory came in the 1940s-1950s. No material milestone by age 26 was found beyond completing his doctorate early.

name: John Tukey
milestone_by_age_26: Tukey earned his PhD from Princeton at age 24 in 1939 and was appointed assistant professor at Princeton in 1941, but his defining work — the FFT, exploratory data analysis — came in the 1950s-60s; no material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in New Bedford, Massachusetts, to parents who were both teachers, Tukey was schooled at home and showed unusual talents from an early age, reading at three and possessing remarkable mental calculation abilities. He entered Brown University in 1933, earned BS and MS in chemistry (1936, 1937), then switched to mathematics at Princeton, completing his PhD in 1939 under Lefschetz. He was awarded the Jacobus Fellowship, Princeton's top graduate fellowship.
family_context_summary: Only child of Ralph H. Tukey and Adah M. Taker, both secondary school teachers. Father had a doctorate in Latin from Yale and was a high school principal; mother was a substitute teacher. Tukey was schooled at home by his mother.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were educators — father had a PhD in Latin from Yale, mother was a teacher — providing a strong educational environment at home, but no documented family expertise in mathematics or science specifically.
evidence_summary: Tukey was clearly gifted — reading at three, home-schooled by teacher parents, PhD from Princeton at 24, Jacobus Fellowship — but his defining contributions (the FFT with Cooley in 1965, exploratory data analysis, box plots) came decades later. His early topology work was competent but not landmark. No material milestone by age 26 was found beyond completing his doctorate.

name: James Cooley
milestone_by_age_26: By age 26 (1952), Cooley had a BA from Manhattan College (1949) and an MA from Columbia (1951); his defining work — the Cooley-Tukey FFT algorithm — was published in 1965 at age 39; no material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in Queens, New York, Cooley served in the U.S. Army Air Corps (1944-45) before attending Manhattan College on the GI Bill, graduating with a BA in 1949. He earned an MA in mathematics from Columbia University in 1951 and worked as a programmer at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton (1953-1956) on von Neumann's IAS machine. His PhD in applied mathematics from Columbia was completed in 1961.
family_context_summary: Born in New York City to Anna Fanning and William Francis Cooley. Grew up in the Woodside neighborhood of Queens. Served in the U.S. Army Air Corps after high school.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources as having direct family domain expertise in mathematics or computing.
evidence_summary: Cooley's early career was that of a competent programmer and applied mathematician. His landmark contribution — the Cooley-Tukey FFT algorithm published in 1965 — came at age 39, well after 26. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: R. W. Hamming
milestone_by_age_26: By age 26 (February 1941), Hamming was still a graduate student; his PhD was completed in June 1942 at age 27, and his defining Hamming code work came in 1947 at age 32; no material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in Chicago, Illinois, Hamming attended three junior colleges before receiving a scholarship to the University of Chicago, where he earned his BS in mathematics in 1937. He earned an MA from the University of Nebraska in 1939 and a PhD from the University of Illinois in 1942. After teaching briefly at Louisville, he joined the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos in 1945 and then Bell Labs in 1946, where he developed error-correcting codes.
family_context_summary: Born in Chicago to Richard J. Hamming and Mabel G. Redfield. Father was Dutch and ran away from home at sixteen to fight in the Boer War. Mother's lineage goes back to the Mayflower. Family was not wealthy; attended junior colleges due to Depression-era financial difficulties.
parent_family_domain_summary: No documented family domain expertise in mathematics or computing. Father's background was military; mother's lineage was early American.
evidence_summary: Hamming's path through University of Chicago, Nebraska, and Illinois was a standard academic trajectory. His PhD was completed at 27, just after the age-26 cutoff. His landmark error-correcting codes were developed at Bell Labs in 1947 when he was 32. No material milestone by age 26 was found.
